gloss: stir up, trouble; bring disaster on
summary: עָכַר is to stir up and so to trouble: to bring disaster on a household, a camp or a land, as Simeon and Levi did on Jacob by making him stink among the Canaanites (Gen 34:30), and Achan on Israel by taking of the devoted thing (Jos 6:18; 7:25). Scripture names the troubler by his deeds: not Elijah but Ahab, who forsook Yahweh’s commandments (1Ki 18:17–18), and the man greedy of gain or cruel, who troubles his own house and flesh (Pro 11:17; 15:27). Achan’s valley was called עֵמֶק עָכוֹר, the valley of Trouble (Jos 7:26), which Yahweh promises to make a door of hope (Hos 2:17). Arabic ʿakira, with the same ʿ, is “become turbid, dreggy”, and its derived forms “make turbid” and “become confused, embroiled”.

words.gloss: stir up, trouble; bring disaster on

senses.gloss: bring trouble on a people, house or land
senses.definition: By one’s own deed to bring disaster on the community one belongs to: to make it hated, liable to attack or to Yahweh’s anger, or to weaken it.

evidence.note: Jacob to Simeon and Levi: עֲכַרְתֶּם אֹתִי, “to make me stink among the inhabitants of the land … they will gather against me and smite me, and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.” The trouble is spelled out.
Taking of the devoted thing would “make the camp of Israel a חֵרֶם and trouble it”: one man’s theft puts the whole camp under the ban.
Joshua to Achan: מֶה עֲכַרְתָּנוּ, “why have you troubled us?”, after Israel’s defeat at Ai (Jos 7:5, 11–12).
“Achar, the troubler of Israel (עוֹכֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל), who trespassed in the devoted thing.”
Jonathan: “My father has troubled the land”; Saul’s curse on anyone who ate before evening (1Sa 14:24) left the people faint, while a little honey brightened Jonathan’s eyes.
“He who troubles his own house will inherit wind.”
“He who is greedy of gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live”: troubling set against living.

senses.definition: To bring grief or harm on a person, or on oneself; of Yahweh, to bring on the troubler the trouble he caused.

evidence.note: “The man of kindness does good to (גֹּמֵל) his own soul, but the cruel troubles (עֹכֵר) his own flesh”: the opposite of doing good.
Jephthah to his daughter, bound by his vow: “you have brought me very low, and you are among those who trouble me (בְּעֹכְרָי).”
יַעְכֳּרְךָ יַהְוֶה בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה, “Yahweh will trouble you this day”: the troubler is repaid in kind, and stoned.

senses.definition: The participle as a title: the one whose deeds have brought disaster on the people.

evidence.note: Ahab to Elijah, after three years of drought: הַאַתָּה זֶה עֹכֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל, “Is it you, troubler of Israel?”
Elijah: “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken the commandments of Yahweh and gone after the Baals.”
עָכָר עוֹכֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל: Achan, here spelled Achar, is named by what he did.

senses.definition: Of pain held in, to be stirred up and made worse.

evidence.note: “I was dumb with silence, I held my peace from good, and my pain was stirred up (נֶעְכָּר)”; the heart grows hot within and the fire burns (Psa 39:4).

senses.definition: Of what the wicked gain: to be troubled, to bring trouble with it.

evidence.note: “In the house of the righteous is much treasure, but in the revenue of the wicked is trouble (נֶעְכָּרֶת)”; compare Pro 15:27, greed troubling the house.
Jesus is accused before Pilate: “We found this one διαστρέφοντα the nation”, the charge Ahab laid against Elijah.
Paul to Elymas: “will you not cease διαστρέφων the right ways of the Lord?”
Every soul that will not hear the prophet like Moses ἐξολοθρευθήσεται from the people.

opposites.note: The kind man does good to his own soul; the cruel troubles his own flesh.
The greedy troubles his house; he who hates bribes will live.

phrases.gloss: one who troubles his own house

words.gloss: trouble (only in the valley’s name, עֵמֶק עָכוֹר)
words.summary: Used only as the name of a valley, עֵמֶק עָכוֹר, “the valley of Trouble”, which the text explains from the verb: the place where Achan, who troubled Israel, was troubled by Yahweh and stoned.

senses.definition: The valley where Achan was stoned, named for the trouble he brought on Israel and Yahweh brought on him; it lay on Judah’s northern border, and the prophets make it a place of rest and hope.

evidence.note: Achan and all that was his are brought up to עֵמֶק עָכוֹר.
After “Why have you troubled us? Yahweh will trouble you” (Jos 7:25), a heap of stones is raised, Yahweh turns from his anger, “therefore the name of that place is called עֵמֶק עָכוֹר to this day.”
A point on the border of Judah, going up toward Debir.
“I will give her … עֵמֶק עָכוֹר for a door of hope (פֶּתַח תִּקְוָה)”: trouble turned to its opposite.
“Sharon shall be a fold of flocks, and עֵמֶק עָכוֹר a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me.”

opposites.note: The valley of Trouble given as a door of hope.

phrases.gloss: the valley of Achor, the valley of Trouble

words.summary: Once, beside the serpent, a creature whose venom is under the lips. It has four letters, and how it is formed from עכר, if it is, is not understood; no cognate sharing its meaning has been found, so its tie to the root rests on the filing alone.

senses.definition: A creature with venom, set in parallel with the serpent, as a picture of wicked men’s tongues.

evidence.note: “They sharpen their tongue like a serpent (נָחָשׁ); the venom of an עַכְשׁוּב is under their lips.”
Paul quotes the line, “the poison of asps (ἀσπίδων) is under their lips”, among the verses showing that all are under sin.
ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη αὐτῶν, quoting Psa 140:4.

parallels.note: The serpent, beside the עַכְשׁוּב, for the tongue of the wicked.

cognates.gloss: become dreggy, turbid; make turbid; become confused, embroiled together
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give ʿakira of water, wine and oil “became dreggy, or feculent, thick, or turbid”; forms II and IV “he rendered it dreggy, or turbid”, “put into it dregs”; form VIII of darkness “became confused”, and of people “became confused, or mixed together, in war, … embroiled together in contention”; the noun ʿakar is “dregs, lees, sediment”. Stirring up what has settled answers to Hebrew עָכַר “stir up, trouble”, and the confusion of people to the troubling of a community. Arabic ʿ (ع), not ġ (غ), stands behind ע. Lane also lists ʿakara “turn back, return (against an adversary)” in the same root, whose link to the Hebrew is not evident.

cognates.gloss: stir up, make turbid; (passive participle) troubled, of the mind; (ithpeel) be disturbed, spoiled
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic: stirring earth into water to make it turbid (Nidd. 20a), a mind troubled (Men. 53a), and in the Targums for Hebrew עָכַר at Gen 34:30 and (ithpeel) Pro 15:6. Aramaic ע does not show whether ʿ or ġ stands behind it.

evidence.note: Targ. Gen. 34:30; Nidd. 20a; Men. 53a; Ithpe. Targ. Prov. 15:6.
Rabbinic Hebrew of wine and water made turbid and clear again (Gen. R. s. 80, on Gen 34:30), the same physical sense.

doctrine.statement: Ahab calls Elijah “troubler of Israel”, and Elijah answers that the troubler is Ahab and his father’s house, who forsook Yahweh’s commandments and followed the Baals (1Ki 18:17–18). The verses name the troubler by what he does: Achan who took of the devoted thing (Jos 7:25; 1Ch 2:7), the greedy of gain and the cruel (Pro 15:27; 11:17). And the trouble returns on him: “Why have you troubled us? Yahweh will trouble you this day” (Jos 7:25). The same charge was laid on Jesus, “we found this one perverting the nation” (Luk 23:2, with the Greek by which 1Ki 18:18 is rendered), and on Paul and Silas, “these men exceedingly trouble our city” (Act 16:20; 17:6); Paul writes to the Galatian ecclesias that the one who troubles them “shall bear his judgment” (Gal 5:10). From the verses: the one who brings trouble on the people is the one who leaves Yahweh’s commandments, not the one who calls them back, though the faithful are the ones accused of it; and the troubler’s own trouble comes back upon him.

The valley of Achor was named for the trouble Achan brought on Israel and Yahweh brought on him; there the heap of stones was raised and “Yahweh turned from the fierceness of his anger” (Jos 7:24–26). Hosea, speaking of Israel after her unfaithfulness, has Yahweh say that he will lead her into the wilderness and speak to her heart, and give her “the valley of Achor for a door of hope”, and she will answer as in the day she came up out of Egypt (Hos 2:16–17). Isaiah sets the same valley, with Sharon, as resting ground for flocks and herds “for my people who have sought me” (Isa 65:10), in the new heavens and new earth Yahweh creates, where Jerusalem is a rejoicing (Isa 65:17–18). From the verses: the place that stood for Israel’s sin and its judgment, where Yahweh’s anger was turned away, becomes the entrance to their hope when he brings his people back; trouble dealt with is where hope begins.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Lev 23 / Num 10 (the name עָכְרָן, Num 10:26). The database keys the root עכר, as asked. Left out: the names עָכְרָן Ochran (p.cq.ad, in names/ochran.json), עָכָר Achar (p.cq.ac, 1Ch 2:7, filed by the database under root עכנ with Achan; TIPNR Achan@Jos.7.1; not written here) and עֻלָּא Ulla (p.cq.ah, 1Ch 7:39; the database files it under עכר only by BDB’s page order; it is not formed from this root and needs its own name entry under another root). עָכוֹר (p.cq.ab) is kept as a word, since its one use is a place name that Jos 7:25–26 explains from the verb; places get no name entry. עַכְשׁוּב (p.cq.ae) is kept with its link unclear; leads not followed: Arabic ʿankabūt “spider” (Lane p. 2177, root عنكب) and Hebrew עַכָּבִישׁ “spider”, to which some relate it by metathesis. Not followed: Syriac ʿkar “hinder” (Payne Smith not consulted; SEDRA has no ʿkr root in the Peshitta NT); no Akkadian, Ugaritic or South Arabian cognate found (Biella’s ʿkry is “rents”, unrelated). Septuagint renderings not recorded because no New Testament use ties to them: μισητόν (Gen 34:30), ἐκτρίβω (Jos 6:18), ἀπαλλάσσω (1Sa 14:29), ἐξολλύω (Pro 11:17; 15:27), and ἀνακαινίζω for the niphal at Psa 39:3 (used at Heb 6:6 in an unrelated sense). Psa 39:3 and Hos 2:17 are Hebrew verse numbers (English 39:2, 2:15). Open: ἐξολοθρεύω is a weak bridge (Act 3:23 quotes Deu 18:19 / Lev 23:29, not a verse with עָכַר); drop it if the reviewer prefers. The doctrine ‘troubler-of-israel’ cites Act 16:20, 17:6 and Gal 5:10, which use other Greek words (ἐκταράσσω, ἀναστατόω, ταράσσω), as parallel accusations, not as renderings.
